- The experiment with high substrate (S=5.0) successfully separated the models, bringing M17 (product-dependent deactivation of catS) and M16 (substrate-dependent deactivation of catS) to the top, followed by M5, M7, and M11.
- My aim was achieved as the NLL spread has widened significantly. The models are now distinguished by how they handle the accumulation of species (either S or P) during the reaction.
- The current top model (M17) suggests that the catalyst deactivates by reacting with the product, whereas the close second (M16) suggests it deactivates by reacting with excess substrate.

<hypothesis>
To definitively discriminate between product-induced deactivation (M17) and substrate-induced deactivation (M16, M11), we should introduce a high initial concentration of product. 
By running an experiment with a moderate substrate concentration (S = 1.0), standard catalyst (cat = 0.05), and the maximum allowed initial product (P = 0.5), we can directly test the effect of product on the initial state of the catalyst.
- For M17 (P + catS => inactive), starting with P = 0.5 will cause immediate and rapid irreversible deactivation of the catS complex from t=0. This will manifest as a severely stunted initial rate and a very early plateau in conversion.
- For M16 (S + catS => inactive) and M11 (S + cat => inactive), the presence of initial product does not cause irreversible deactivation. The reaction will proceed with an initial rate similar to the baseline (run 1), only slightly slowed by standard thermodynamic reversibility, and will reach a much higher conversion than M17.
- For M5 (catS + cat <=> catP + cat; catP <=> P + cat), the high initial product will shift the final equilibrium towards the catP intermediate, sequestering the catalyst. This will lower the overall rate but will not cause irreversible deactivation, leading to a distinct kinetic profile from M17.
- For M7 (S + catS <=> catS2 => P + catS), the initial product will have minimal effect, and the reaction will proceed rapidly.
</hypothesis>
